text.p: Here are the highlights from Swiss

- Unemployment in Switzerland's building sector rose by another two percent or 524 persons in February. Joblessness climbed by 1.5 percent in the service sector and by 2.1 percent in the health industry.
- The cantons Basel-Stadt and Basel-Land want to cut the number of hospital beds in their region by 600 by the year 2002 in order to lower costs and keep health insurance premiums down.
- The Swiss National Bank will issue a new yellow ten-franc note that depicts Charles Edouard Jeanneret, a.k.a. Le Corbusier, a renowned 20th century architect, urbanist and painter, on April 8.
- Brewer and beverage group Feldschloesschen-Huerlimann suffered a loss in sales and market share in 1996.

- Swiss government opens door for marketing of genetically altered soy beans and derivitive products to start immediately by rejecting an appeal to ban the foodstuffs. - Nearly 1,000 Swiss men had filed applications for civil rather than military service by the end of February, five months after the law was changed to offer an alternative to mandatory armed duty in the country's militia army.
- Genetically altered food products will not be sold in Swiss stores for the next few months due to boycotts by Swiss firms
- ABB Switzerland posted a one percent drop in sales, nine percent decline in orders and a 36 percent fall in net profit in for the 1996 fiscal year compared to 1995.
- A total of 223 million Swiss francs of chocolate was sold in Switzerland in 1996, some two percent more than in 1995. Per capita consumption rose by 100 grams to 3 kilos.

- Vetropack's 1996 profit fell to 0.5 million Swiss francs compared to 9.6 million in 1995 due to extraordinary costs. - Engineering group SIG registered a 26.4 percent rise in profit to 88.6 million Swiss francs in 1996.
